title.en: The Woman Who Went Down to Panoi in Her Body

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XV

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XV 'Death, Burial, After Death'

summary.en: A woman who much desired to see her lately dead brother perfumed herself with water in which a dead rat had been steeped, pulled up a bird's-nest fern, and descended by the hole she had opened. She found Panoi without difficulty, saw friends who never discovered she was alive, found her brother lying in a house — a recent ghost not strong enough to move about — and he cautioned her to eat nothing there; she returned. In Panoi the dead of violent deaths are fenced apart by the manner of their killing, and life there is eternal, unless as some say there are two Panois, one below the other: from the lower the dead never die, but turn into white ants' nests.
summary.zh: 班克斯群島有一婦人，極想見新亡的弟弟。她以浸過死老鼠的水沐浴，使自己帶上死人之氣；又拔起一叢鳥巢蕨，從挖開的洞口走了下去。她毫不費力便到了帕諾伊，遇見故友，無人識破她是活人；弟弟因是新鬼，尚無力走動，正躺在一間屋裡。他囑咐她什麼都不許吃，她便回來了。帕諾伊之中，橫死之人各按死法分圍而居：中箭者一處、中咒者一處、被棒擊者一處——屋中若聞沙沙聲如箭桿相擊，便說是『撥箭之鬼』。帕諾伊之生永無終期；也有人說上下有兩個帕諾伊：死者自上帕諾伊死入下帕諾伊，如生人死離陽世；自下帕諾伊則永不死，只化作白蟻巢。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Codrington 1891); Banks Islands heritage. Descent cluster.

passages.text: Descents to Panoi have been by no means uncommon. There was a woman, who died not many years ago, who once much desired to see her lately dead brother; she perfumed herself with water in which a dead rat had been steeped, to give herself a death-like smell, pulled up a bird's-nest fern, and descended by the hole she had opened. She had no difficulty in finding Panoi, and she saw friends there who were surprised to see her, and never discovered that she was alive. She found her brother lying in a house, because as a recent ghost he was not strong enough yet to move about. He cautioned her to eat nothing there, and she returned. This descent was in the body, as was that of one Molborbor of Valuwa, who went down and saw his wife; but a man in Motlav, more lately dead, used to go down in sleep, his soul descending, and his body remaining as in a trance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: He could do this at will, and received money for doing it, professing to visit the recently dead, about whom their friends were unhappy, and even to be able to bring them back. He never did in fact bring any back; he said he had seen the persons and talked with them, but was prevented from bringing them back. He, too, prepared for his soul's descent by washing his body with water in which a putrid rat, snake or lizard had been steeped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: There are compartments, enclosures fenced apart, in Panoi, in which those who have died violent deaths keep together; those who have been shot are in one place together, those who were charmed to death in a second, those who have been clubbed in a third together. Those who have been shot keep rattling the reeds of the arrows they were shot with; hence if a rat is heard in a house making that kind of noise the saying is that it is a reed-rattling ghost. Life in Panoi is eternal, unless indeed, as some say, there are two Panois, one below the other, and the dead die from the upper to the lower, as living men die from earth; from the lower they never die, but turn into white ants' nests.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Vanvanvegirgir and the Widower in Panoi
title.zh: 范氏引魂下冥：斷腕之妻

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫特拉夫島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XV

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XV 'Death, Burial, After Death'

summary.en: Vanvanvegirgir of Motlav once took down with him, soul and body, a widower who had lost his wife: the man washed himself with the liquor of a putrid black gecko, and was given a stick. In Panoi the ghosts detected the living man and cried 'The smell of that world!' — and tested them with dead men's bones, which they rattled rightly, by one, by two, by three. The wife was brought; she said return was impossible and gave him a shell armlet — and when he took her hand and dragged her, the hand came off and the body came to pieces: the ghost in Panoi has a lanpei, a body with form, colour, and consistency, but not in the world.
summary.zh: 莫特拉夫島的范氏能引魂下帕諾伊。一次他帶上一位喪妻的鰥夫：那人以腐臭黑壁虎之汁淨身，攜一根手杖，隨范氏下界。帕諾伊的亡靈一嗅便叫：『陽世的氣味！』二人自辯亦是死人；亡靈便取出死人的骨頭，叫他們像鬼那樣一根、兩根、三根地撥弄——撥對了，方許前行。范氏尋來其妻；夫妻相見，情話綿綿，丈夫求她同返陽世；她說斷不可能，只贈貝釧一枚留念。丈夫執其手拖拽——那隻手竟脫落，全身散架。緣故是：帕諾伊中的亡靈尚有形有色、有質之地；一回到陽世，便只剩個影子般的廓形。

passages.text: There was a man in former days at Motlav, Vanvanvegirgir by name, who going down to Panoi in his nuieyi, soul, took once another man with him in his body. This man had lately lost his wife, and went to Vanvanvegirgir to enquire about her. He was instructed to give himself the appropriate smell with the liquor of a putrid black gecko, and was given a stick. The two then descended, and reached Panoi; the ghosts detected the living man, and cried out, 'The smell of that world!' The two declared that they were really dead, and to try them the ghosts brought out dead men's bones, to see if they would rattle them as ghosts do, by one, by two, by three; they did this rightly and were allowed to go on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Vanvanvegirgir went forward to find the man's wife, and brought her to him; they talked together, and the man begged her to go back to the world with him. That she said was impossible, and she gave him a shell armlet by which to remember her. He took her by the hand and began to drag her; her hand came off, and her body came to pieces. For, as the story is explained, ghosts in Panoi have something more of body and substance than they have when they come back into the world; else the man could not have taken hold of his dead wife's hand. When a ghost comes into the world, it is but a tapangiu that is seen, a something circumscribed by an outline like a shadow; but the ghost in Panoi has a lanpei, a body, which has not only form and colour, but a certain consistency.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Journey of the Dead on Maewo

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded (native account) by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XV

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XV 'New Hebrides. Journey of the Dead'

summary.en: When the soul leaves the body on Maewo it mounts into a bird's-nest fern, sits among the fronds, and laughs at the people crying over him — 'Who is it they are sorry for? Here am I' — then runs his gardens and paths, the stone of thought, the ravine that must be cleared at a leap, and the revenge of those he wronged on the way, to the three leaping-places at the northern point, one for men, one for women, one for ulcerous persons; at Banoi stands Gaviga, the chief of Banoi, and Matamakira with sharp spears, and a huge fierce pig that devours all who never planted the emba, the pandanus of the mats.
summary.zh: 馬埃沃人相信：靈魂一離身體，便爬上鳥巢蕨，坐在葉間對著哭喪的眾人發笑——『哭什麼？可憐誰？我在這裡呢。』肉身不過是脫下的衣裳。此後靈魂走過自家園圃與舊路，至『思之石』處稍歇：若此時想起孩子、妻子或產業，便會跑回去復活。那裡還有兩巖夾一深澗：一躍而過者永死；躍不過者復生。亡者一路奔跑，生前被他殺害冤枉的鬼魂沿途復仇，棒打刀刺，罵道：『你在世上自以為好漢，如今我們報仇了！』北端有斷崖三處跳臺——男子的、女子的、患瘡者的；墮下者摔碎仍跑，至聖山陶烏——下界之洞的入口。洞前，波諾伊之主加維加與脾氣暴躁的馬塔馬基拉持長矛刺戳新鬼；還有一頭巨豬，吞食一切生前不曾種過織席露兜樹的人——種過的方可攀上樹頂避豬。故人人爭種露兜。未穿耳者不得飲水，未文身者不得食美餐；未入蘇蓋會社的亡靈，只能像狐蝠般倒掛樹上。

sensitivity.note: Native Maewo/Tanoriki account translated by Codrington (1891); living after-death belief.

passages.text: In the first place, they think that when the soul, famani, leaves the body in death, it mounts into a tree in which is a bird's-nest fern, and sitting among the fronds, laughs and mocks at the people who are crying and making great lamentations over him. There he sits, wondering at them and ridiculing them. 'What are they crying for?' he says; 'who is it they are sorry for? Here am I.' For they think that the real thing is the soul, and that it has gone away from the body just as a man throws off his clothes and leaves them, and the clothes lie by themselves with nothing in them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891), after a native Maewo account; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the soul goes through his gardens and along his customary paths, and finally leaves the place. He runs along the line of hills till he reaches the end of the island, and there he comes to the place of recollection, the stone of thought; if he remembers there his child or his wife or anything that belongs to him, he will run back and come to life again. In the same place also are two rocks with a deep ravine between them; if the ghost clears this as he leaps across he is for ever dead, but if one fails he returns to life again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891), after a native Maewo account; not verbatim.

passages.text: The ghost pursues his course running along the mountain range to the end opposite to Raga, Pentecost, at the land's end, or brink of sea, and when he arrives safely all the ghosts of those who have died before assemble and receive him joyfully. They believe also that as he runs the ghosts of those whom he has wronged in this world, whom he has foully slain by club or arrow, or has killed by charms, take a full revenge upon him, beating him, tearing him, and stabbing him with daggers, such as men stick pigs with; one of them will say to him, 'While you were still in the world you thought yourself a valiant man; but now we will take our revenge upon you.' Another path of the ghosts takes them to the northern point of Maewo, where there is a deep gully and three leaping-places, one for men, one for women, and one for ulcerous persons. It is a curse to wish a man may fall down there; if a ghost falls in leaping he is smashed to pieces, but runs on and comes to the hill Tawu, which is very sacred to ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891), after a native Maewo account; not verbatim.

passages.text: Here is Gaviga, a vui, the chief of Banoi, and Matamakira, or Salolo as the Tanoriki people say, a quarrelsome and ill-tempered man on earth; these stand with large and sharp spears and try to stab the new-comers. There is a huge fierce pig also there, which will devour all who have not in their lifetime planted the emba, pandanus, from which mats are made. If one has planted such he can climb up out of the reach of the devouring beast, and for this reason every one likes to plant that tree. Here also, if a man's ears are not pierced, he is not allowed to drink water; if he is not tattooed, he must not eat good food. Here the ghosts of those who have not joined the Suqe hang like flying foxes upon the trees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891), after a native Maewo account; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bound Husband of Garat: Pay Your Debts
title.zh: 加臘特山上被縛的亡夫

region.en: Mount Garat, Gaua, Banks Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島高阿島加臘特火山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XV

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XV 'Death, Burial, After Death'

summary.en: A woman of Vanua Lava whose Gaua husband died fell very ill and appeared to die; she recovered and told the people she had followed him to the hill Garat and seen him there bound hand and foot. The ghosts told her this was done because he had not paid his debts: 'Go back to the Gaua people and say to them, Pay your debts, don't kill one another; this is how we shall treat such men.'
summary.zh: 瓦努阿瓦島一名婦人，其夫為高阿島人，亡故之後她重病垂危，狀若已死；卻又醒轉，對眾人說：她隨亡夫到了加臘特山，親眼見他在那裡被捆住手腳。亡靈們告訴她，這是因為他生前賴賬未償——『回去對高阿人說：把債還清，不要自相殘殺；我們就是這樣對付這種人的。』

passages.text: There is still living in Vanua Lava a woman who turned her descent to Panoi to a useful purpose. Her husband, a Gaua man, died, and she herself was very ill and appeared to die. She recovered, however, and told the people that she had followed her husband to the hill Garat, and had seen him there bound hand and foot. The ghosts told her, she declared, that this was done because he had not paid his debts; 'Go back,' they bade her, 'to the Gaua people, and say to them, Pay your debts, don't kill one another; this is how we shall treat such men.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XV (1891); not verbatim.
